linkedin.text:
Visa and Mastercard's proposed swipe-fee deal has its final hearing Monday, 21 years after merchants first sued.
If it's approved, a lot of small shops on flat-rate pricing may never see the cut.

The deal trims the card-issuing banks' part of the fee on Visa and Mastercard credit cards by 0.1 percentage point for 5 years. On a $40 haircut paid by one of those cards, for example, that's about 4 cents.

Whether you get it depends on how you're priced. If your processor passes card fees through at cost plus a set markup (often called interchange-plus), the lower bank fee reaches you automatically. If you pay one flat or tiered rate, it stays where it is unless your processor lowers it. Network fees and the markup sit on top either way. The deal has other terms too, like letting shops turn down some premium cards.

About 1,000 merchants, Walmart among them, asked Judge Brian Cogan to say no; they say the cut only takes rates back to their 2023 level. The ruling may come after Monday, and it can be appealed.

I'd take the 4 cents, and I'd want every shop to know whether it's getting them. That's part of why I started SVPay: when customers pay with SVPay instead of a card, the shop pays no processing fee and $0 to cash out, and SVPay makes money from paid software plans, never from a cut of your sales. Customers pay no SVPay fee to pay a shop; adding money with a card or Apple Pay carries Stripe's fee.

So this week, ask your processor one thing: which pricing am I on?

#SmallBusiness #Payments

facts.text: The interchange-fee litigation against Visa and Mastercard dates to 2005 (Payments Dive: 'litigation dating to mid-2005'; 'The litigation dates to 2005')

Visa-Mastercard Rule 23(b)(2) settlement, In re Payment Card Interchange Fee and Merchant Discount Antitrust Litigation, MDL 1720 (E.D.N.Y.): preliminary approval June 9, 2026 by U.S. District Judge Brian Cogan; final approval hearing set for Monday, Nov 16, 2026 in Brooklyn; not yet final. Re-checked Nov 12, 2026: the Nov 11 report still lists the Nov 16 hearing. The official settlement site (www.interchangeequitablereliefsettlement.com) could not be fetched from this run (client error), and PACER is not reachable, so the status rests on the two reports.
Judge Brian Cogan granted preliminary approval on June 9, 2026
The settlement would trim credit interchange (swipe) fee rates by 10 basis points, 0.1 percentage point, for five years

It would impose a 1.25% rate for standard consumer cards for eight years (Payments Dive: a 1.25% rate for standard consumer cards, in its paragraph on credit interchange; Reuters: standard consumer rates capped at no more than 1.25%). Interchange is the part of the swipe fee paid to the card-issuing banks, so the posts call it the card-issuing banks' part of the fee
It would give merchants the right to decline some higher-cost Visa and Mastercard premium and commercial credit cards
Merchants would gain new rights to add surcharges and offer discounts for credit cards (they can already surcharge credit cards within state law and network caps; the posts say more room)
Walmart and about 1,000 other merchants asked the judge to reject final approval (978 signers on the Sept 10 objection letter, plus Walmart)
Merchant objectors say the rate cut 'would merely return the average Visa/Mastercard rate to its 2023 level' (paraphrased in the posts, no quotation marks)
facts.quote: would merely return the average Visa/Mastercard rate to its 2023 level

facts.text: Final approval can be appealed: the 2nd Circuit overturned an earlier settlement in this litigation in 2016, and the current deal must still survive appeals; Monday is the hearing and the ruling may come later
Visa and Mastercard urged the court to grant final approval (filing a month before the Nov 16 hearing)

Whether a shop sees an interchange cut depends on its pricing: on interchange-plus (pass-through) pricing the lower interchange flows through; on flat-rate or tiered pricing the rate moves only if the processor lowers it; network fees and the processor's markup sit on top of interchange
The settlement cuts Visa and Mastercard credit interchange; it does not cover debit, American Express or Discover
Merchants first sued in 2005; the final approval hearing is Monday, Nov 16, 2026 before Judge Brian Cogan

SVPay customers pay no SVPay fee to pay a shop; adding money with a card or Apple Pay carries Stripe's fee (founder decision Nov 8, 2026, via the coordinator); shops pay 0% processing fees and $0 to cash out on payments made with SVPay
Worked example: $500,000 a year in credit card sales x 0.1 percentage point = $500 a year, if the full cut reaches the shop's rate
0.1 percentage point of $10,000 is $10
Merchants paid a 2.35% fee on Visa and Mastercard transactions in 2024 (weighted average, Nilson Report)
Example: the 2.35% average falling 0.1 percentage point to 2.25%
Example: 0.1 percentage point of a $40 haircut paid by Visa or Mastercard credit card is about 4 cents

The cut is to credit interchange, the card-issuing banks' part of the swipe fee, which Visa and Mastercard set; processors add their own markup, and flat-rate pricing moves only if the processor lowers it
SVPay home page: what the customer pays

SVPay pricing (approved line, checks/approved_lines.json pricing_one_line): 0% processing fees and $0 to cash out on payments made with SVPay, on every plan; SVPay makes money from paid software plans
